\chapter{The Whole Set, And How Much Of It}
\label{ch:el-conjunto-y-el-resto}
\hlchaptermodality{352}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el conjunto, entero, la mayoria, el resto and escaso, and say why a whole thing is one nobody has touched.}

Complete ES-C352-escaso: name a set, say it is whole, name most of it, name what is left, and say there is not enough.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el conjunto]{el conjunto — the set, and the yoke that holds it}

\label{lesson:ES-C352-conjunto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{several}, then \emph{triple}. (\emph{Varios}; \emph{el triple}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la gente — one sort of group.
  \item todo — the whole this names.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kon-JUN-to}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{j} is the scraped \emph{jota}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el conjunto} — \textquotedblleft{}the set,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the whole group taken as one.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{iungere} meant \emph{to yoke} — to put two oxen under one wooden beam so they must pull together. Add \textbf{com-}, \emph{together}, and you get \textbf{coniungere}, and its participle \textbf{coniunctus}: yoked as one.

That is what a set is. Not things that happen to be near each other, but things counted as a unit because somebody has put them under one yoke.

English took \emph{iungere} by every road. A \textbf{junction} is where roads are yoked. A \textbf{joint} is where bones are. \textbf{Conjunction} is the grammar word for a yoking word — \emph{y}, \emph{o}, \emph{pero}. \textbf{Adjoin}, \textbf{subjugate} and \textbf{junta} all follow.

And the root reaches much further east. Sanskrit \textbf{yoga} is the same ancient word, and it means a \emph{yoking} too — of body to breath, or of a mind to its task.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A name for a group of things, before we start dividing it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el conjunto}
  \item \emph{un conjunto de libros}
  \item \emph{todo el conjunto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{iungere} mean? (To yoke.) And which eastern word for a discipline is the same yoking? (Yoga.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[entero]{entero — whole, meaning nobody has touched it}

\label{lesson:ES-C352-entero}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{triple}, then \emph{the set}. (\emph{El triple}; \emph{el conjunto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item todo — the nearest word you already have.
  \item poco — what is left if this fails.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en-TE-ro}, three beats with the weight on the second. One tapped \emph{r}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{entero} — \textquotedblleft{}whole,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}entire.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{integer} is \textbf{in-}, \emph{not}, plus a form of \textbf{tangere}, \emph{to touch}. A whole thing is one that \textbf{nobody has laid a hand on} — nothing broken off, nothing taken.

Spanish has two words where English has one feeling. \textbf{Todo} is the whole counted up: all of it. \textbf{Entero} is the whole left unbroken: none of it missing. \emph{Todo el libro} is every page; \emph{el libro entero} is the book with no page torn out.

English took \emph{integer} twice. Once through French, worn down to \textbf{entire}. Once straight from Latin, kept whole, for a number with no fraction on it — an \textbf{integer}. \textbf{Integrity} is a character nobody has tampered with, and to \textbf{integrate} is to make a thing whole again.

\emph{Tangere} on its own gives \textbf{tangent}, \textbf{tangible} and \textbf{contact}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A set, and a way to say the set is still complete.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{entero}
  \item \emph{el libro entero}
  \item \emph{un día entero}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two Latin pieces make \emph{integer}? (\emph{In-}, not, and \emph{tangere}, to touch.) And what is an \textbf{integer} in arithmetic? (A number with no fraction on it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la mayoría]{la mayoría — most of them, and the greatness inside a mayor}

\label{lesson:ES-C352-mayoria}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the set}, then \emph{whole}. (\emph{El conjunto}; \emph{entero}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el maestro — a cousin of this word.
  \item mucho — the vaguer way to say a lot.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ma-yo-RÍ-a}, four beats with the weight on the third. The written accent on the \emph{í} keeps it from folding into the \emph{a}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la mayoría} — \textquotedblleft{}most of them,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the majority.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{magnus} was \emph{great}, and its comparative \textbf{maior} was \emph{greater}. Spanish softened the \emph{-ai-} into \emph{-ayo-} and got \textbf{mayor}, then hung the abstract ending on it: \textbf{mayoría}, \emph{the greater part}.

Notice that it is a comparison, not a count. A \emph{mayoría} is not a number; it is whichever side is larger.

English holds the family in several shapes. A \textbf{major} is the greater sort. A \textbf{mayor} is the greater man of a town. \textbf{Majesty} is greatness worn in public. \textbf{Magnitude}, \textbf{magnify} and \textbf{maximum} come off \emph{magnus} itself.

And you have a cousin already. \textbf{El maestro} goes back to Latin \textbf{magister}, \emph{the greater one} — the man who was more than the rest of the room, which is what a teacher was supposed to be.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word for the larger share of a set.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la mayoría}
  \item \emph{la mayoría de la gente}
  \item \emph{la mayoría de los libros}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does Latin \emph{maior} mean? (Greater.) And what was a \emph{magister}, word for word? (The greater one in the room.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el resto]{el resto — what is left standing}

\label{lesson:ES-C352-resto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{whole}, then \emph{most of them}. (\emph{Entero}; \emph{la mayoría}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item otro — the others this gathers up.
  \item estar — the verb standing inside it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{RES-to}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} at the start of a word is rolled. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el resto} — \textquotedblleft{}the rest,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the remainder.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{restāre} is \textbf{re-}, \emph{back}, plus \textbf{stāre}, \emph{to stand}. What \textbf{stands back} when the others have gone is what is left over.

That verb is becoming an old friend. It is inside \textbf{estar}, inside \textbf{la estación}, inside \textbf{el instante}. Here it is again, standing still while the count moves on without it.

English \textbf{rest}, in the sense of \emph{the remainder}, is this word — and it has nothing to do with the other English \emph{rest}, the one that means sleep, which is a Germanic word about a resting-place on a journey. Two words, same spelling, no relation.

To \textbf{arrest} somebody is to make them stand still. Something \textbf{restive} will not move. A \textbf{residue} is what stays behind.

It comes with \emph{de} behind it: \textbf{el resto de la gente}, the rest of the people.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The larger share, and everything that is not in it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el resto}
  \item \emph{el resto de la gente}
  \item \emph{el resto del día}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{restāre} mean, word for word? (To stand back.) And are the two English \textbf{rest}s related? (No — one is Latin standing, one is Germanic sleeping.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[escaso]{escaso — scarce, because the good parts were picked out}

\label{lesson:ES-C352-escaso}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{most of them}, then \emph{the rest}. (\emph{La mayoría}; \emph{el resto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item poco — the plain word this sharpens.
  \item bastante — the opposite end of the scale.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{es-KA-so}, three beats with the weight on the second. Both \emph{s} sounds are clear, never buzzed. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{escaso} — \textquotedblleft{}scarce,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}in short supply.\textquotedblright{}

\textbf{Poco} says \emph{there is little}. \textbf{Escaso} says \emph{there is less than there ought to be} — the word carries a shortfall in it.

Behind it is a late Latin \textbf{excarpsus}, from \textbf{carpere}, \emph{to pluck}, with \textbf{ex-}, \emph{out}. What is \emph{escaso} is what is left after the good parts have been plucked out of it. A picked-over heap.

\emph{Carpere} is a fine root to own. An \textbf{excerpt} is a passage plucked out of a book. A \textbf{carpet} was plucked wool before it was a floor. And \textbf{carpe diem} is not \emph{seize the day} so much as \emph{pluck the day}, the way you pick fruit that will not keep.

English \textbf{scarce} is the same \emph{excarpsus}, arriving through Old French \textbf{escars} — so \emph{escaso} and \emph{scarce} are one word, and the Spanish shape is the more conservative of the two.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A whole set, its larger share, its remainder, and the word for when there is not enough of it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{escaso}
  \item \emph{el agua está escasa}
  \item \emph{poco o escaso}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{carpere} mean? (To pluck.) And what is an \textbf{excerpt}, word for word? (A passage plucked out.)
\end{tcolorbox}
